content: The text provided appears to be a list of references from a scientific or medical document, formatted in a way that includes publication details, authors, and study titles. 1. In 2015, the Pangaea Global AIDS Foundation conducted a preliminary report on community consultations for the WHO's updated consolidated treatment guidelines. This report explored the acceptability of early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and viral load monitoring, focusing on the values and preferences of both service users and providers. 2. Gupta et al. (2011) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate early mortality among adults initiating ART in lowand middle-income countries. The study, published in PLoS One, highlighted the challenges and outcomes associated with ART initiation in resource-limited settings. 3. Brinkhof et al. (2009) compared the mortality rates of HIV-infected patients starting ART in sub-Saharan Africa with those of HIV-unrelated mortality. Their findings, published in PLoS Medicine, provided critical insights into the impact of ART on survival in this region. 4. Vitoria et al. (2014) emphasized the importance of simplifying antiretroviral therapy as a necessary step in the public health response to HIV/AIDS in resource-limited settings. Their work, published in Antiviral Therapy, underscored the need for streamlined treatment approaches. 5. The WHO's 2013 consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection provided recommendations for a public health approach. These guidelines aimed to optimize treatment strategies globally. 6. The SMART Study Group (2008) analyzed major clinical outcomes in ART-naive participants and those not receiving ART at baseline. Published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases, the study highlighted the benefits of early ART initiation. 7. Cohen et al. (2011) demonstrated the prevention of HIV-1 infection through early ART initiation in their study published in the New England Journal of Medicine. This landmark research provided evidence for the role of ART in reducing transmission. 8. Grant et al. (2015) examined the association between baseline viral load, CD4 count, and week 4 virologic response with virologic failure in the ACTG Study A5202. Their findings informed strategies for optimizing ART outcomes. 9. Sterne et al. (2009) conducted a collaborative analysis of 18 HIV cohort studies to determine the timing of ART initiation in AIDS-free HIV-1-infected patients. Published in The Lancet, the study provided evidence for early treatment benefits. 10. Ahdieh-Grant et al. (2003) used a cohort approach to evaluate when to initiate highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Their findings, published in the American Journal of Epidemiology, contributed to understanding optimal treatment timing. 11. Althoff et al. (2010) explored virologic and immunologic responses to HAART by age and regimen class. Published in AIDS, the study highlighted the variability in treatment outcomes across different patient demographics. 12. The ART Cohort Collaboration (2003) analyzed the prognostic importance of initial response in HIV-1-infected patients starting potent ART. Published in The Lancet, the study emphasized the significance of early treatment response. 13. The ART Cohort Collaboration (2009) investigated the effect of baseline CD4 cell counts on the clinical significance of short-term immunologic response to ART in individuals with virologic suppression. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 14. The CASCADE Collaboration (2011) examined the timing of HAART initiation and its impact on clinical outcomes in HIV-1 seroconverters. Published in the Archives of Internal Medicine, the study provided evidence for early treatment initiation. 15. Cozzi-Lepri et al. (2001) analyzed data from the ICONA study to determine when to start HAART in chronically HIV-infected patients. Published in AIDS, the study offered insights into treatment timing and outcomes. 16. Egger et al. (2002) conducted a collaborative analysis of prospective studies to assess the prognosis of HIV-1-infected patients starting HAART. Published in The Lancet, the study highlighted survival benefits associated with early treatment. 17. Garcia et al. (2004) evaluated long-term CD4+ T-cell responses to HAART based on baseline CD4+ T-cell counts. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study provided evidence for the importance of baseline immune status. 18. Gras et al. (2007) demonstrated that achieving CD4 cell counts of 800 cells/mm³ or greater after seven years of HAART is feasible for most patients starting with 350 cells/mm³ or greater. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 19. The HIV-CAUSAL Collaboration (2010) analyzed the effect of combined ART on overall mortality in HIV-infected individuals. Published in AIDS, the study underscored the life-saving potential of ART. 20. The HIV-CAUSAL Collaboration (2011) investigated the timing of combined ART initiation to reduce mortality and AIDS-defining illnesses in developed countries. Published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, the study provided evidence for early treatment initiation. 21. Kitahata et al. (2009) compared the effects of early versus deferred ART initiation on survival in HIV-infected individuals. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the study highlighted the survival benefits of early treatment. 22. Krishnan et al. (2011) analyzed the incidence of non-AIDS-defining cancers in ART-naive subjects after ART initiation. Published in Oncology, the study provided insights into cancer risks in HIV-infected individuals. 23. Merito and Pezzotti (2006) compared the costs and effectiveness of different starting points for HAART in HIV-positive patients. Published in the European Journal of Health Economics, the study informed cost-effective treatment strategies. 24. Opravil et al. (2002) evaluated the clinical efficacy of early HAART initiation in asymptomatic HIV-infected patients with CD4 cell counts >350 cells/mm³. Published in AIDS, the study supported early treatment benefits. 25. Palella et al. (2003) examined the survival benefits of initiating ART in HIV-infected individuals across different CD4+ cell strata. Published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, the study emphasized the importance of early treatment. 26. Phillips et al. (2001) analyzed HIV viral load responses to ART based on baseline CD4 cell counts and viral load. Published in JAMA, the study provided evidence for personalized treatment approaches. 27. Plettenberg et al. (2011) assessed the impact of earlier HAART initiation on immune status and clinical outcomes in treated patients. Published in Infection, the study highlighted the benefits of early treatment. 28. Gallant et al. (2015) explored health outcomes associated with the timing of ART initiation. Their findings emphasized the importance of early treatment for improved outcomes. 29. The When to Start Consortium (2009) conducted a collaborative analysis of 18 HIV cohort studies to determine the timing of ART initiation in AIDS-free HIV-1-infected patients. Published in The Lancet, the study supported early treatment initiation. 30. Stover et al. (2014) analyzed the impact and cost of the 2013 WHO recommendations on ART eligibility. Published in AIDS, the study highlighted the economic and health benefits of expanded treatment coverage. 31. Tanser et al. (2013) demonstrated that high ART coverage is associated with a decline in HIV acquisition risk in rural KwaZulu-Natal. Published in South African Science, the study emphasized the public health impact of ART. 32. He et al. (2013) showed that ART reduces HIV transmission in discordant couples in rural Yunnan, China. Published in PLoS One, the study provided evidence for the preventive benefits of ART. 33. Kato et al. (2013) evaluated the potential impact of expanding ART and combination prevention in Vietnam. Published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, the study highlighted strategies for HIV elimination. 34. Eaton et al. (2014) analyzed the health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of earlier ART eligibility and expanded treatment coverage. Published in The Lancet Global Health, the study supported earlier treatment initiation. 35. Siedner et al. (2015) conducted a meta-analysis of trends in CD4 counts at care presentation and treatment initiation in sub-Saharan Africa. Published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, the study highlighted the persistent issue of late presentation. 36. Kiertiburanakul et al. (2014) examined trends in CD4 cell count levels at ART initiation and factors associated with late initiation among Asian HIV-positive patients. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study provided regional insights. 37. Ford et al. (2015) addressed the persistent problem of late presentation to care and immunodeficiency at ART initiation. Published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, the study emphasized the need for earlier diagnosis and treatment. 38. Fleischman et al. (2010) analyzed the economic burden of late entry into medical care for HIV-infected patients. Published in Medical Care, the study highlighted the cost implications of delayed treatment. 39. Mocroft et al. (2013) identified risk factors and outcomes for late presentation in HIV-positive individuals in Europe. Published in PLoS Medicine, the study provided evidence for targeted interventions. 40. Holmes et al. (2014) discussed the health system implications of the 2013 WHO consolidated ART guidelines and strategies for successful implementation. Published in AIDS, the study emphasized the importance of health system strengthening. 41. Hirschhorn et al. (2012) addressed the challenge of managing cancer and other noncommunicable chronic diseases in older people living with HIV/AIDS in resource-limited settings. Published in AIDS, the study highlighted the need for integrated care. 42. Haregu et al. (2012) reviewed the epidemiology of HIV/AIDS and noncommunicable disease comorbidity in developing countries. Published in the Journal of Global Health Care Systems, the study emphasized the growing burden of comorbidities. 43. Nigatu (2012) discussed the integration of HIV and noncommunicable diseases in health care delivery in lowand middle-income countries. Published in Preventing Chronic Disease, the study highlighted the need for comprehensive care models. 44. The ART Cohort Collaboration (2010) analyzed causes of death in HIV-1-infected patients treated with ART between 1996 and 2006. Published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, the study provided insights into mortality trends. 45. Rodger et al. (2014) presented findings from the PARTNER Study, showing that HIV transmission risk through condomless sex is negligible if the HIV-positive partner is on suppressive ART. The study was presented at the 21st Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections. 46. The TEMPRANO ANRS 12136 Study Group (2015) conducted a trial of early ART and isoniazid preventive therapy in Africa. Published in The Lancet, the study demonstrated the benefits of early intervention. 47. Jia et al. (2013) evaluated the use of ART to prevent HIV transmission in serodiscordant couples in China. Published in The Lancet, the study provided evidence for the effectiveness of treatment as prevention. 48. Jose et al. (2014) analyzed laboratory adverse events and therapy discontinuation based on CD4+ cell counts at ART initiation. Published in AIDS, the study highlighted the importance of monitoring and managing side effects. 49. Le et al. (2013) demonstrated enhanced CD4+ T-cell recovery with earlier HIV-1 ART initiation. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the study supported early treatment for improved immune recovery. 50. Okulicz et al. (2015) examined the influence of ART timing on the potential for immune status normalization in HIV-1-infected individuals. Published in JAMA Internal Medicine, the study emphasized the benefits of early treatment. 51. Schneider et al. (2013) analyzed the impact of health care payer type on HIV stage at ART initiation in the USA. Published in AIDS Care, the study highlighted disparities in access to care. 52. Donnell et al. (2010) conducted a prospective cohort analysis of heterosexual HIV-1 transmission after ART initiation. Published in The Lancet, the study demonstrated the preventive benefits of ART. 53. The INSIGHT START Study Group (2015) evaluated the initiation of ART in early asymptomatic HIV infection. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the study provided evidence for early treatment benefits. 54. Cohen et al. (2015) presented the final results of the HPTN 052 randomized controlled trial, showing that ART prevents HIV transmission. Published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society, the study confirmed the role of treatment as prevention. 55. The UNAIDS Gap Report (2015) provided a comprehensive overview of the global HIV epidemic, highlighting gaps in treatment and prevention efforts. 56. Irvine (2015) explored values and preferences regarding the timing of ART initiation, emphasizing the importance of patient-centered care. 57. Arreola et al. (2015) examined the impact of sexual stigma, criminalization, and investment on access to HIV services among men who have sex with men worldwide. Published in AIDS Behavior, the study highlighted barriers to care. 58. Mahajan et al. (2008) reviewed the literature on stigma in the HIV/AIDS epidemic and provided recommendations for addressing this persistent issue. Published in AIDS, the study emphasized the need for stigma reduction strategies.
